course.title: Colon cancer
course.html:
Anatomy

  • Located between ileo-cecal valve and colorectal junction
  • Divided into caecum, ascending colon, hepatic flexure (or right flexure), transverse colon, splenic flexure (or left flexure), descending and sigmoid colon
  • Sigmoid colon continues with rectum at colorectal junction
  • Arterial: SMA = “ right colon” (caecum, ascending colon, right flexure and right half of transverse colon)
    • ileo-colic, right colic and middle colic a.

IMA = “ left colon” (left half of transverse, left flexure and descending colon)

  • left colic artery and sigmoid a.
  • Veins: Right colon → follow arteries and drain into superior mesenteric vein and further in portal vein Left colon → follow arteries and drain into inferior mesenteric vein and splenic vein or portal vein
  • Lymphatics also follow vascular branches
  • Ascending and descending colon attached to posterior abdominal wall by Told’s fascia → non mobile
  • Only transverse colon and sigmoid colon are mobile and can be used for anastomosis and stomas

Avascular areas

Colon/ rectum covered by serosaColon/ rectum without serosa
= intraperitoneal
- Cecum, Transverse, Sigmoid
- Anterior descending
- Anterior ascending
- Rectosigmoid
- Upper third and anterior wall of middle third of rectum
→ Those subsites must invade the serosa before
spreading to adjacent tissues and/or organs		- Posterior ascending
- Posterior descending
- Lower third of rectum (rectal ampulla)
→ Invasion into adjacent organs and tissues occurs
without peritoneal involvement

Epidemiology and etiology

  • Rising incidence in developed countries
  • Peak incidence 70-80 y
Risk factorsColorectal CAMetastasis
- Age > 50y
- Previous polyp → adenomatous ≥ 2cm
- IBD
- Family history (FAP, Gardner’s, HNPCC)
- Personal history of bowel CA
- Diet (animal fat, meat and low fibers
→ promote anaerobic bac. → bile salts
transformed into carcinogens)
- Exercise
- Obesity
- Smoking and alcohol		- Synchronous → 3-12%
- Metachronous → 3%
- Other polyps → 30%		- Up to 70% of pat. with colorectal CA
develop liver metastasis
- 50% are isolated liver metastasis
- 25% are synchronous
- 5-10% are resectable
HereditarySporadic
-
-		FAP- Environmental factors
HNPCC

* hereditary non polyposic colorectal cancer

  • 5-10% of colon CA
  • Familial clustering
  • If they don’t fit a defined syndromes → micro-satellite instability (mis-match repair)
  • All need surveillance
FAPHNPCC
- Autosomal dominant
- Malignancy occurs at age of 30
- > 100 adenomatous polyps and
microadenomas in the large intestine
- 100% cancer risk at age of 40
- Gardner syndrome – associates besides familial
polyposis, desmoid tumors located in midgut or
abdominal wall and bone tumors
Diagnosis based on
→ Polyps
→ Family history
→ Confirmed by identification of mutation
Management
- Colectomy
+ IRA (ileorectal anastomosis)
+ IAP (ileoanal pouch)
+ Ileostomy
→ 30% risk by 60 y
→ Don’t forget desmoids and duodenal tumors
→ Don´t forget rectal CA		- Lynch syndrome I and II
- NO polyps
- 90% risk of developing CA
- Lacks clear phenotypic characteristics
Diagnosis based on
→ Family history (Amsterdam criteria (specific, not sensitive)
or Bethesda criteria) and earlier age of onset (< 45 y)
→ Demonstration of defective MMR (MSI)
→ Confirmed by identification of mutation
- Genes implicated → MSH2, 6/ MLH1, 3/ PMS2, 1/ TGFBR2
Lynch syndrome I → familial colon cancer
Lynch syndrome II → HNPCC assoc. with other cancers of
GI tract or reproductive system
Management
- Annual colonoscopy
- CA125
- CT

IRA

IAP

Amsterdam I criteria→ 3 relatives (linked) with CRC → 1 is 1st degree relative
→ 2 generations of CRC
→ 1 CRC before age 50y
→ FAP is excluded
Amsterdam II criteria→ > 3 relatives diagnosed with HNPCC related cancers (CRC, endometrial, small
bowel, ureter, renal pelvis), one of them is 1st degree relative
→ 2 generations of CRC
→ 1 CRC before age 50y
Modified Bethesda criteria→ Individuals in families that meet Amsterdam criteria
→ Individuals with 2 HNPCC-related cancers including synchronous and
metachronous CRC or assoc. extracolonic cancers
→ Individuals with CRC and a 1st degree relative with CRC and/or HNPCC

Cancer development

Normal epithelium → APC loss → hyperproliferation → early adenoma → K-ras mutation → intermediate adenoma

  • chromosome 18 loss → late adenoma → p53 loss → cancer
  • Polyp removal leads to CRC prevention = prophylaxis !
  • Polyp is surrogate marker
Adenomatous polyps
→ benign, BUT high risk of
developing into
adenocarcinoma over time		- After 10-15 years evolution → cancer
- High risk polyps
→ Flat
→ Villous
→ 3 or more
→ > 1 cm
→ High grade dysplasia
- Colonoscopy
→ Long term surveillance
- Low risk = 1-2 polyps < 1cm → 5 years until negative/ none
- Intermediate = 3-4 small or 1 polyp > 1cm → 3 years until 2- ve
- High risk > 4 or > 2 polyps > 1 cm → 1 year then 3 years
Inflammatory bowel syndrome- 1% per year over 10 years
- Extensive colitis
- Colonoscopy surveillance
- Proctocolectomy for
→ Cancer
→ Severe dysplasia

Pathomorphology

  • Vegetating, ulcerative vegetating or infiltrating (scirrhous) tumor
  • Mostly adenocarcinoma
  • Rarely - mucinousor anaplastic carcinomas, sarcomas or lymphomas

Symptoms (exam !!!)

Ascending colonDescending colonGeneral
- Anemia
- Palpable tumor
- Diarrhea
- Fever		- Obstruction
- Altered bowel habit/ transit
- Tenesmus
- Pain
Rectosigmoidian syndrome:
rectorrhagia; tenesmus;
blood, pus or mucus in stool		→ Malignant syndrome
- Weight loss
- Loss of appetite
- Low grade fever
- Pallor, Fatigue

Dissemination pathways

  • Direct invasion through wall into other organs/ carcinomatosis/ Krukenberg tumors/ Blumer's shelf
  • Lymph node metastasis
  • Portal vein/ hematogenous metastasis (to liver and lung)
  • Intraluminal seeding (metastatic tumors further down in colon)

Complications

  • Jaundice, hepatomegaly → liver metastasis (rarely lung metastasis)
  • Ascites, carcinomatosis nodules → peritoneal carcinomatosis
  • Peritonitis → perforations (especially of caecum (diastatic perforation))
  • Intestinal obstruction → obstructing tumor (more common in left/ descending CRC)
  • Hemorrhage → anemia
  • Neighbor organ invasion (colo-vesical and colo-vaginal fistulas)

Investigations and staging

Colonoscopy and biopsyVisualization, location, + treatment of potential pre-neoplastic pathology
Blood samplesLiver and kidney function, diabetes, CBC, tumor markers
Chest X rayLung metastasis
Barium enemaLocation, specify no. of lesions, stenosis, NO biopsy
USUSColon wall thickening → not specific; peritumoral collections due to
perforation; liver metastasis or carcinomatosis
CT (+ contrast)Location, stenosis, presence of complications (perforation, obstruction),
presence of intraabdominal injuries (liver metastasis, carcinomatosis);
Virtual colonoscopy BUT NO biopsy or treatment
MRISame details as CT
PETDetecting metastasis and relapse after radical treatment; NOT routinely
CEACEAUsed to monitor postoperative colon cancer
→ Measured pre- and post-op reevaluated at predetermined time range
→ if ↓ = treatment was radical; if ↑ = relapse, metastasis

DD

Ascending colonDescending colon
- Pseudo tumoral form of appendicitis
- Appendicular tumors
- CD
- Ileo-cecal tuberculosis
- Other intra-abdominal tumors		- Diverticular disease
- Granulomatous colitis
- Other intra-abdominal tumors

Colon cancer staging

  • Duke staging
  • Confined to bowel wall Dukes’ A → 85%
  • Through wall Dukes’ B → 65%
  • Spread to lymph nodes Dukes’ C → 35%
  • Spread to liver (metastasis) Dukes’ D → 10%
  • TNM staging
Primary tumor (T)
TXPrimary tumor cannot be assessed
T0No evidence of primary tumor
TisCarcinoma in situ: intraepithelial or invasion of lamina propria
T1Tumor invades submucosa
T2Tumor invades muscularispropria
T3Tumor invades through the muscularispropria into the pericolorectal tissues
T4aTumor penetrates to the surface of the visceral peritoneum
T4bTumor directly invades or is adherent to other organs or structures
Regional lymph nodes (N)
NXRegional lymph nodes cannot be assessed
N0No regional lymph node metastasis
N1Metastasis in 1-3 regional lymph nodes
N1aMetastasis in 1 regional lymph node
N1bMetastasis in 2-3 regional lymph nodes
N2Metastasis in 4 or more lymph nodes (N2a – 4-6 LN; N2b →7 LN)
Distant metastasis (M)
M0No distant metastasis
M1Distant metastasis

Treatment

Radical
Palliative
→ unresectable
  • 1) Preparation for surgery
  • Informed consent
  • Stoma counselling
  • Bowel preparation → Fortrans, Macrogol
  • Thromboembolism prophylaxis
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis
  • 2) Radical surgical treatment
  • For R0 resection → 10 cm margins in both directions + removal of mesocolon + lymphadenectomy
Right hemicolectomy= resection of last loop of ileum, caecum, ascending colon, right colic flexure
and first third of transverse colon
- Restoring digestive transit through ileo-transverso-anastomosis
- Indicated for tumors in caecum until proximal third of transverse colon
Extended right hemicolectomy- Segmental colectomy on transverse colon with colo-colic anastomosis
- Indicated in tumors located in the second third of transverse colon
Left hemicolectomy= resection includes distal third of transverse colon, left colonic flexure,
descending colon with/without sigmoid, completed with
transverso-sigmoido-anastomosis or transverso-rectal anastomosis or
terminal colostomy and closing distal stump
- Indicated in tumors located from left colonic flexure to descending colon or
sigmoid
Extended left hemicolectomy- Spleenic flexture tumors
- Uncommon
Segmental colectomy- Tumors on second third transverse colon
- Resection of transverse colon with colo-colic anastomosis
Sigmoidectomy- Tumors located in sigmoid colon
- Colorectal anastomosis or terminal colostomy with closure of rectal stump
(Op. Hartmann)
High anterior resection
Limited left or right resection

Lymph nodes: Epicolic, Paracolic, Intermediate colic, Superior mesenteric nodes, Inferior mesenteric nodes

  • ➔Since left hemicolectomy goes together with inferior artery resection → complete oncologic resection
  • ➔Since right hemicolectomy uses only resection of some arteries → incomplete oncologic resection
  • 3) Palliative stomas and bypass
ColostomyLateral/ LoopTerminal/ end
TemporaryProtective colostomyOP Hartmann *
DefinitivePalliative treatmentRectal resection

Lateral colostomy Terminal and loop colostomy

1: Ileostomy

2: Colostomy (transverse colon or sigmoid colon → movable)

  • Transversostomy, Sigmoidostomy

* Only for sigmoid colon, often used in emergencies

  • Ileo transverso anastomoses for cancers located between caecum and proximal third of transverse colon
  • Transverso sigmoido anastomosis for cancers located between distal third of transverse colon and descending colon

4)

Endoscopic treatment- Useful in patient with obstruction due to tumor
- Inserting trans-tumoral stent to release obstruction
- By this method the patient can be operated in a single surgical procedure,
not in successive surgeries
- In addition, patient could be operated as elective surgery, after preparation, not as
emergency
Oncologic treatment- Chemotherapy that is given before surgery (neoadjuvant) or postoperative
(adjuvant) depending on tumor staging
- Some single-agent chemotherapy: 5-FU, Vincristine, Irinotecan, Oxaliplatin,
Capecitabine, Bevacizumab, and Cetuximab
- But most often multiagent chemotherapy: FOLFIRI: folic acid, 5-FU, Irinotecan;
FOLFOX: Oxaliplatin, 5-FU, Leucovorin; 5-FU with Vincristine
Radiation therapy- Not used for colon cancer, only for rectal cancer
ImmunotherapyImmunotherapy→ Levamisole or Interferon, may be given in conjunction with 5-FU chemotherapy
- Make sure immunotherapy is first course treatment

5)

Obstructing cancer

  • Presentation at more advanced stage
  • Survival rate worse → More aggressive tumors
  • Bypass, Stoma or Stent

Perforation with/ without diastatic obstruction

  • Operative mortality = 30-40%
  • 5-year survival rate = 7-15%
  • Colonic resections with colostomy
  • 6) Post-op complications
  • most important one = anastomotic fistula → may lead to peritonitis
  • Was reduced by pre-op colon preparation and use of mechanical staplers

Follow-up

  • At least for 2 years
  • at 3 months - abdominal US, Chest X-ray and CEA
  • at 6 months - CT and colonoscopy
  • After initial 2 years an annual follow-up should be done until 5 years

Screening

  • Population = simple, cheap, reliable, safe, acceptable
  • High risk → Positive FH, FAP, IBD, Adenomas

Population screening

  • Endoscopic removal of adenomas >1cm reduces risk
  • Population screening improves survival
  • Detection of adenomas and early cancers
  • Carcinomas most prevalent at 65-75 yrs
  • Adenomas most prevalent at 55-65 yrs
  • Aim screening at 50/ 55-75 y.
  • Flexible sigmoidoscopy

course.title: Benign colonic disorders
course.html:
Ulcerative colitis

  • Causes ulcers in lining of rectum and colon
  • Can happen at any age, but usually between 15-30 y.
  • More frequent in women
  • Family history (20% hereditary)
  • Jewish population
  • Smoking has protective factors ! (DD for CD)

Pathomorphology

  • Macroscopic appearance
  • Initial phases: diffuse erythema and hyperemia with granular mucosa
  • Advanced stage: friable mucosa, nodular erythematous appearance and inflammatory pseudopolyps
    • ulcerations and bleedings
  • Worst at distal colon/ rectum (sparing of rectum = DD for CD)
  • Lesions are continuous without normal areas in between (DD to CD)
  • Microscopic appearance
  • Wide spectrum of areas with acute and chronic inflammation appearance, distorted and dilated crypts with abscesses, infiltrated and thickened muscularis mucosae
  • Limited to mucosa (DD for CD)

Etiology

  • Still unknown
  • Vascular (ischemia), autoimmune, immunological bacterial interactions, allergic mechanisms, genetic

Symptoms

  • Intensity of clinical signs and symptoms usually reflects extension and severity of colic mucosal lesions !
  • Usually has intermittent evolution with periodic exacerbations and remissions
  • Yet, 10% have continuous progressive evolution which does not respond to medical treatment
CommonLess common
- Abdominal pain
- Diarrhea
- Weight loss
- Rectal bleeding and mucus		- Poor appetite
- Fever, night sweats
- Rectal pain

I) Ulcerative proctitis = inflammation limited to rectum (15 cm above anal verge)

  • Often mild, intermittent rectal bleeding (rectorrhagy) is only symptom
  • If more severe → rectal pain, urgency, tenesmus, diarrhea
  • DD: infective proctitis (biopsy), CD (anal fistulas are not present in UC), ischemic proctitis, post-radiation proctitis,

proctitis secondary to colostomy

  • Rarely extends upstream
  • Usually does not requires surgical treatment

II) Proctosigmoiditis = inflammation of rectum and sigmoid colon (25-30 cm from anal verge)

  • rectal bleeding, urgency, tenesmus, bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain/ cramps, fever, weight loss
  • Harvesting multiple biopsies is paramount as macroscopic lesions can be exceeded by microscopic ones (reflecting

real extension of disease !)

III) Left-sided colitis = inflammation from rectum to left colon

  • bloody diarrhea, abdominal cramps, weight loss, left-sided abdominal pain

IV) Pancolitis or universal colitis = inflammation affecting entire colon

  • bloody diarrhea very frequent, abdominal pain and cramps, weight loss, fatigue, fever, night sweats, anemia,

dehydration

V) Fulminant colitis = rare but severe form of pancolitis

  • Pat. are extremely ill with anemia, dehydration, severe abdominal pain, protracted diarrhea + bleeding, shock
  • Risk of developing toxic megacolon and colon perforation

Extraintestinal manifestations

  • Arthritis and spondylitis → HLA-B27
  • Dermatological lesions = nodular erythema, gangrenous pyodermitis
  • Ocular lesions = uveitis, episcleritis, keratoconjunctivitis
  • Hepatic = primitive sclerotic cholangitis !

Colitis activity assessment → Truelove and Witts Severity Index

MILDSEVEREFULMINANT
Stools (#/day)<4>6>10
Blood in stoolIntermittentFrequentContinuous
Temp° CNormal< 37.5> 37.5 (fever)
PulseNormal> 90> 90 (tachycardia)
HemoglobinNormal (> 11)< 75 % of normal (< 11)Transfusion required
ESR (mm/h)< 30> 30> 30
RadiographyNormalThumbprintingDilated colon
Abdominal examNormalTender, no reboundDistended, +/- rebound

Complications

  • Persistent hemorrhage with consequent anemia
    • Ulcers larger > 5 mm in diameter or of > 10 ulcers of any diameter over a 10 cm colon length
    • spontaneous hemorrhage = criteria for severe form!
  • Fulminant colitis and Toxic megacolon
    • 10-13% of cases
    • 5-44% mortality!
    • Tachycardia and fever (negative role of corticotherapy → suppress clinical picture and “hide” perforation)
    • Repeated plain abdominal X ray, ultrasound, CT important for evaluation of efficacy of treatment
    • Dilation of transverse colon > 6 cm, loss of haustrations = radiological criteria for toxic megacolon
    • High risk of perforation
  • Perforation
    • Increase in body temp. and appearance of colic pneumatosis on X ray → indicate imminence of perforation
  • Stenosis
    • In time colon becomes rigid, shortened, haustrations disappear, stenoses, local smooth muscle hypertrophy
    • Stenotic areas usually do not exceed 2-3 cm
    • Stenoses longer > 5 cm, more likely malignant !
  • Cancer
    • 3-5 fold increased risk

Risk factors include

  • extensive involvement of colon (pancolitis)
  • evolution > 3 years
  • onset in childhood or adolescence
  • Even patients with asymptomatic pancolitis/ colo sigmoiditis require periodic endoscopy

Toxic megacolon

  • Dilation > 5.5 cm on X-ray
  • Fever (38.5°C)
  • Tachycardia (120)
  • Leukocytosis (10.5)
  • Anemia
  • Dehydration
  • State of consciousness
  • Electrolytes
  • Hypotension

Etiology

  • CD
  • Colitis due to Clostridium difficile
  • Other infectious diseases → Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, CMV assoc. with HIV, amoebae
  • Ischemic colitis
  • Ineffective peristalsis → paralysis of myenteric plexus
  • Distension leads to perforation
  • Sepsis and death

Imaging

  • Colonoscopy + biopsy (s. pathomorphology)
  • Barium enema: not routinely performed anymore, but number of elements are characteristic - initial rigidity and

diminished distendibility of inflamed segment, effacement of haustrations, “tubularization”, shortening/ retraction of colon, mucosa takes granular, nodular appearance, ulcers, continuity from rectum all the way upstream

DD

  • Crohn’s disease !
  • Dysenteries
  • Rectal/colic malignancy

Treatment

Conventional therapies

  • 5-ASAs/ sulfasalazine !
  • Corticosteroids !
  • Azathioprine/ 6-mercaptopurine, Methotrexate, Cyclosporine, Infliximab

Management of fulminant colitis and toxic megacolon

General- I.v. fluid and correction of electrolytes
- Complete bowel rest
- Discontinue anticholinergics, antidiarrheals, narcotics !
- Rule out infectious diseases
Decompression- Rectal tube
- Nasogastric or long nasointestinal tube
Medical care- I.v. corticosteroids for inflammatory bowel disease
- Broad spectrum antibiotics
Surgical intervention- Failed medical care after 48-72 h
- Progressive toxicity or dilation
- Signs of perforation
- Pre-pubertal children

Surgery

  • Curative resection ! (unlike in CD)
  • Removes threat of life-threatening complications
  • Obviates need for medical therapy
  • Reasonable quality of life
  • Indications for elective surgery
    • 1. Lack of response to medical treatment
    • 2. Malignization
    • 3. Increased risk of malignization (dysplasia)
    • 4. Extra intestinal manifestations
    • 5. Stature weight retardation in children
  • Indications for emergency surgery
    • 1. Fulminant colitis resistant to medical treatment
    • 2. Toxic megacolon
    • 3. Perforations, abscesses
    • 4. Important hemorrhage
    • 5. Acute bowel obstruction
  • 1) Elective surgery
    • Total proctocolectomy + ileostomy: resection of entire colon and rectum, ileal stump externalized, mesentery is keept (in contrast to cancer)
    • Total colectomy + ileo-recto anastomosis: less frequent, mild or no rectal involvement, disadvantages - appearance of ulcerative proctitis, risk of malignization and great number of soft stools
    • Total colectomy + stripping of rectal mucosa and ileo-rectal anastomosis: s. oben + detachment and excision of rectal mucosa over 5-6 cm above dentate line
    • Ileostomy: terminal, continent reservoir (Koch), J or S or W shaped reservoir
  • 2) Emergency surgery
    • Subtotal colectomy + ileostomy

Success rates not perfect

  • 64% clinical remission
  • 23% “rescue” colectomy
  • 30-40% of those hospitalized with acute, severe colitis require colectomy

Predictors of colectomy

  • > 8 stools/ day
  • Increased CRP
  • > 3 stools/ day after 3rd day of admission
  • 85% colectomy

Complications in colon surgery

  • UTI retention
  • Significant hypokalemia
  • Ileus
  • GI tract → abscess, leak, SBO
  • Cardiac
  • Atelectasis (requiring bronchoscopy)
  • Pneumonia

Colonic diverticulosis

  • Affects 50% of individuals > 60 years → only 20% develop symptomatic disease
  • Prevalence among females and males similar, males present at younger age
  • Diverticulosis is rare in underdeveloped countries, where diets include more fiber
  • Pseudodiverticulum → involves only protrusion/ herniation of mucosa through muscularis propria of colon
  • Occurs at point where vasa recti penetrate through muscularis propria up to peritoneal serosa
  • Diverticula commonly affect sigmoid, followed by descending colon (high-pressure zone)

Pathogenesis

  • Chronic intracolonic overpressure (chronic constipation (low fiber diet))
  • Collagen defect or other disturbances of colonic parietal structure

Clinically

  • Mainly asymptomatic
  • Abdominal discomfort, borborygmus, change in rhythm and nature of defecation
  • Crampy pain in left iliac fossa; may last for hours or days
  • Being exacerbated by food and partially relived by defecation or gas emission

Complications

  • Diverticulitis = inflammation of diverticulum due to retention of particulate material within diverticular sac and

formation of fecalith

Acute uncomplicated diverticulitisComplicated diverticulitis
- Fever
- Leukocytosis
- Anorexia
- LLQ abdominal pain
- Obstipation
- Localized or generalized peritonitis
- Air-fluid level in LLQ on plain abdominal film		- Peridiverticular abscess
- Perforation → free → peritonitis (rare)
→ localized → abscess
- Stricture/ stenosis → partial or even complete obstructions
- Fistula (perforations usually occur gradually and colonic
segments become sticky due to inflammation → erosion into
vagina, urinary bladder, small intestine or skin)
  • Vasa recti are eroded by fecalith → bleeding
  • Most common cause of hematochezia in patients > 60 y
  • Increased risk for bleeding → hypertension, atherosclerosis, NSAIDs
  • Most bleeds are self-limited and stop spontaneously with bowel rest

Hinchey classification system

  • Staging of perforated diverticular disease
Stage IPericolic or mesenteric abscess
Stage IIWalled-off pelvic abscess
Stage IIIGeneralized purulent peritonitis
Stage IVGeneralized fecal peritonitis

Paraclinical diagnosis

Irrigoscopy/- Effective, but nowadays not common anymore
- Barium will opacify diverticula - round, clear-cut, possible fistulas
irrigography
CTCT= best method
- Thickened colonic wall > 4 mm, strictures
- Inflammation within pericolic fat +/- collection of contrast material or fluid (abscess)
Abdominal US- May also provide useful information (colonic wall, intra-abdominal collections, fistulas) at
much lower cost
Colonoscopy- Accurate information regarding mucosal changes, possibly source and therapy of
hemorrhage, but does NOT provide data on pericolic changes
- Extremely important that endocolic pressure during exploration does not increase excessively
(risk of perforation)
- Essential in detection of other concomitant lesions (benign, malignant tumors)
- Followed closely with repetitive colonoscopy, looking for evidence of colonic ischemia
Angiography- Important for source and therapy of massive bleeding
  • Barium enema or colonoscopy should not be performed in the acute setting because of higher risk of perforation
  • Barium enema or colonoscopy should be performed ~6 weeks after an attack of diverticular disease
  • Sigmoid malignancy can masquerade as diverticular disease

DD

  • Ovarian cyst
  • Endometriosis
  • Acute appendicitis
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease

Treatment

Medical treatmentAsymptomatic- Fiber-enriched diet
- Glucagon i.m.
- Avoid nuts and popcorn
Symptomatic
(diverticulitis)		- Bowel rest with water diet
- Antibiotics
- Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole or ciprofloxacin + metronidazole
- Addition of ampicillin for non-responders
- IV piperacillin or oral penicillin/ clavulanic acid
- Nasogastric suction in severe cases
Surgical treatment- 2 attacks of diverticulitis requiring hospitalization
- Not rapidly improve on medical therapy
Goals of surgical management
- Controlling sepsis
- Eliminating complications
- Removing distended colonic segment
- Restoring intestinal continuity
Elective
- Sigmoidectomy
- Left hemicolectomy
+ colorectal anastomosis
Emergency
- Sigmoidectomy
- Left hemicolectomy
+ closure of distal stump and temporary colostomy
- with restoration of digestive tract after 6-8 weeks
Indications for elective surgeryIndications for emergency surgery
- > 2 diverticulitis episodes
- Immunosuppressed
- Long duration of corticosteroid treatment
- First attack of diverticulitis occurring < 40y
- Subocclusive snd.
- Impossibility to exclude cancer
- Fistulas		- Generalized peritonitis (free perforation/ abscess)
- Abundant bleeding
- Intestinal complete occlusion

Options for surgical management

1.Proximal diversion of fecal stream withileostomyorcolostomyandsutured omental patchwith drainage
2.Resectionwithcolostomyand mucus fistula or closure of distal bowel with formation of Hartmann's pouch
3.Resectionwith anastomosis (colo-proctostomy)
4.Resectionwith anastomosis and diversion(colo-proctostomywithloop ileostomy)
  • Patients with presumed bleeding from diverticular disease requiring emergent surgery without localization should

undergo a total colectomy

  • Surgery should be performed if patient is unstable or has had a 6-unit bleed within 24 h
  • Percutaneous drainage recommended for abscesses > 5 cm with well-defined wall that is accessible
  • Paracolic abscesses < 5 cm in size may resolve with antibiotics alone

Contraindications to percutaneous drainage

  • No percutaneous access routes
  • Pneumoperitoneum
  • Fecal peritonitis

without diverting stoma		3.822

book.html:
The colon Benign colonic disorders

ULCERATIVE COLITIS

Doru Munteanu

It is an inflammatory idiopathic disorder that affects the large intestinal mucosa over variable lengths: thus, it can involve the rectum (ulcerative proctitis), the left colon or the entire colon (ulcerative left colitis and pancolitis respectively).

The disease is clinically characterized by diarrhea, abdominal pain and rectal bleedings.

EPIDEMIOLOGY

The incidence of the disease varies from 0.9 to 15.1º/ . Northern

ºººº European countries are the most affected, incidence being on the increase.

  • The incidence of ulcerative colitis (UC) is 30% higher in women.
  • Jewish population seems to be 2-3 times more frequently affected.
  • The hereditary factor is also involved (in up to 20% of cases).

As an environmental factor, patients who quit smoking or non-smokers have a significantly higher risk to develop the disease (in contrast to Crohn’s disease, where smoking is a demonstrated risk factor!).

PATHOMORPHOLOGY

Macroscopic appearance:

  • In the initial phases, endoscopy reveals diffuse erythema and a discrete

vascular pattern, or hyperemia with a granular mucosa.

  • In a more advanced stage, the friable mucosa has a nodular-erythematous

appearance and inflammatory pseudopolyps are present. Subsequently, ulcerations and bleedings occur. The most advanced lesions are usually found in the distal colon/rectum. The sparing of the rectum involves differential diagnosis from Crohn’s disease.

The following are characteristic:

  • the presence of inflammatory pseudopolyps;
  • lesions are continuous in the affected segment, without normal areas between them (as is the case withCrohn’s disease).

Microscopic appearance:

-Colonoscopy reveals a wide spectrum of areas with acute and chronic inflammation appearance, with distorted and dilated crypts, some of them with abscesses, infiltrated and thickened muscularis mucosae.

-Typically, the lesions arelimited to the mucosa.

PATHOGENY is still unknown; the incriminated factors/mechanisms are:

* vascular (ischemia)

* autoimmune

* immunological-bacterial interactions

* allergic mechanisms

* genetic, etc.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS

The more extended and severe the lesions of the colic mucosa are, the more severe and intense the clinical manifestations.

  • Thus, in ulcerative proctitis, the extension of mucosal alterations is

limited (up to 15 cm above the anal verge). It represents about 1/3 of the cases. Manifestations of ulcerative proctitis are usually mild (rectorrhagy– 90%, diarrhea– 50%, rectal tenesmus– 30%).

The differential diagnosis of ulcerative proctitis is made from:

* infective proctitis/colitis.

* Crohn’s disease.

* ischemic proctitis.

* post radiatiotherapy proctitis.

* proctitis secondary to colostomy.

* Infective proctitis/colitis, frequent in homosexual subjects, is diagnosed in the context, by cultures of the responsible pathogenic germ and serological tests. Here, biopsy reveals the absence of crypt distortion.

* In Crohn’s disease, the anus and the perianal region (fistula in ano, abscesses, fissure in ano) are involved, which is not the case in ulcerative proctitis. Fistulisation in adjacent organs, transmural alterations and thickening of the ractal wall are common in Crohn’s proctitis and absent in the ulcerative one.

* Radiation proctitis occurs after pelvic radiation (radiotherapy for advanced rectal or other pelvic malignancies).

* Finally, proctitis may occur 2-3 months after colostomy.

In terms of evolution, ulcerative proctitis rarely extends upstream. It also requires surgical treatment extremely rare.

  • Proctosigmoiditis: lesions extend up to 25-30 cm upstream the anal

verge, involving the rectum and the sigmoid colon. Harvesting multiple biopsies during colonoscopy is of paramount importance, as the extension of upstream macroscopic lesions can be exceeded by that of microscopic ones (reflecting the real extension of the disease !). Isolated rectal bleedings occur in 6% of the cases, while isolated abdominal pain in 14%. In the vast majority of cases however, clinical associations of signs and symptoms, likediarrhea and rectorrhagy (in most of the cases – 75%), along with abdominal pain (50%), fever (25%) and weight loss (40%), help in rising a strong clinical suspicion and further investigations.

Remember, the intensity of clinical signs and symptoms usually

reflects the extension andseverity of the colic mucosal lesions !

  • Pancolitis: mucosal alterations are extended over the entire colon; as a

consequence, due to the large surface of ulcerated and inflamed mucosa, rectal bleedings and diarrhea are more frequent and severe, leading to severe anaemia and dehydration.

RADIOLOGICAL SEMIOLOGY: although radiological investigation (based on barium enema) is not anymore the most relevant diagnostic technique, a number of elements are characteristic for ulcerative colitis. Thus, the initialrigidity and diminished distendibility of the inflamed colic segment, is progressively followed by a gradual effacement of haustrations, with the “tubularization”, rigidization, shortening and retraction of the colon. The mucosa takes a granular, then nodular and reticular appearance. Ulcers occur subsequently. Lesions can be observed in continuity from the rectum all the way upstream.

ENDOSCOPIC SEMIOLOGY: erythema initially appears, with the effacement of the vascular network or hyperemia with granular mucosa; lesions subsequently progress towards a nodular pattern, with erythema and increased friabilityof the mucosa, as well as pseudoinflammatory polyps, while severe ulcers and hemorrhage are found in advanced phases.

CLNICAL EVOLUTION

  • - Acute or severe episodes are characterized by:
  • diarrhea and rectorrhagia, at least 6times a day;
  • fever (<37.5ºC);
  • tachycardia with more than 90 beats/min.;
  • hemoglobin < 11 g/dl and
  • ESR > 30 mm/hour.
  • A mild episode consists of:
  • maximum 4 stools/ day,
  • without fever and tachycardia,
  • hemoglobin > 11 g and
  • ESR < 30 mm/hour.
  • A moderate episode ranges between the two above-mentioned extremes (Edwards and Truelove classification).

UC usually has an intermittent evolution, with periodic exacerbations and remissions. Yet, about 10% of the cases have a continuous progressive

evolution, which does not respond to medical treatment. These are

candidates for colectomy.

COMPLICATIONS include:

  • persistant hemorrhage with consequent anaemia,

- fulminant colitis,

- toxic megacolon,

  • perforation and
  • stenosis.

Ulcers larger than 5 mm in diameter or of more than 10 ulcers of any diameter over a 10 cm colon length, associated with spontaneous hemorrhage,

are criteria for the severe form!

  • Hemorrhage is rarely abundant, but in these cases, emergency surgery

is the only one that can save the patient.

  • Fulminant colitis and toxic megacolon occur in about 10-13% of cases.

It is essential to recognize fulminant colitis before the onset of toxic megacolon (5-44% mortality!). Mortality is much higher after the perforation has developed (up to 65%).

The clinical signs are those of toxicity:

* tachycardia and fever(the negative role of corticotherapy

should be mentioned, as it may suppress the clinical picture

and “hide” the perforation).

Repeated clinical and radiological patient’s supervision (plain abdominalX-ray examinations, ultrasound, CT) is important for the evaluation of the efficacy of treatment:

* The dilation of the transverse colon more than 6 cm in

diameter, the loss of haustrations are radiological criteria that

confirm toxic megacolon).

* The increase in body temperature by 3 tens of degree (under

corticotherapy) as well as the appearance of colic pneumatosis

on radiological examination may indicate the imminence

ofperforation.

In time, the colon becomes a rigid, shortened tube, haustrations disappear, stenoses develop, generated by the important local smooth muscle hypertrophy (unlike Crohn’s disease, in which stenoses have a sclero-fibrotic nature). The presence of ulcerations in stenotic areas that do not exceed 2-3 cm in length is endoscopically characteristic. Stenoses longer than 5 cm, particularly those occurring after a long evolution of the disease, are more likely malignant!

UCERATIVE COLITIS AND CANCER

YES! Patients with ulcerative colitis have a 3-5-fold increased risk to develop a colonic neoplasm. Risk factors include:

  • the extensive involvement of the colon (pancolitis);
  • an evolution longer than 3 years;
  • onset in childhood or adolescence.

This is why even patients with asymptomatic pancolitis or colo-sigmoiditis require periodicendoscopic monitoring (with biopsy), in order to detect initial dysplasia or early neoplasia.

EXTRA-INTESTINAL MANIFESTATIONS:

1.Arthritis/spondylitis occurs in 25%, 3% respectively, of ulcerative colitis cases; the large joints are generally affected; ankylosing spondylitis is associated with the HLA-B haplotype.

27

2.Dermatological lesions (9%) – nodular erythema and gangrenous pyodermitis.

  • Nodular erytema appears as firm erythematous nodules, 1-5 cm in diameter, located on the extensor sides of the legs.
  • Gangrenous pyodermitis starts as a discrete pustule that evolves into deep ulcers.

3.Ocular manifestations (4%) – uveitis, episcleritis and keratoconjunctivitis (manifesting by ocular pain, photophobia, cephalea, vision disorders).

4.Hepatic manifestations – primitive sclerotic cholangitis (initially manifesting by asthenia, pruritus, subsequent abdominal pain, then fever and jaundice). The disease is associated in more than 50% of cases with ulcerative colitis.

The most important DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS is made from Crohn’s disease. The explorations that decide the diagnosis are pancolonoscopy with multiple segmental biopsies and contrast enterography. Several distinctive aspects are noteworthy: the alternation of affected and unaffected colic segments, the normal rectum, as well as the involvement of the small intestine; these morpho-clinical elements exclude the diagnosis of ulcerative colitis.

Dysenteries (especially in extended, severe forms) and, rectal/colic malignancy must be always in the clinician’s mind.

TREATMENT

In cases with limited extension (ulcerative proctitis), 5-aminosalicylic acid suppositories (2-3 times a day) and/or enemas are effective. Sometimes, in the initial phases, hydrocortisone or ACTH enemas also have beneficial effects; this treatment is maintained until remission, after which oral treatment can be initiated.

In extensive forms, the therapeutic pillar consists of sulfasalazine and corticoids.

Oral sulfasalazine associated with local treatment usually controls acute episodes and maintains remissions for one year or longer. In cases that do not respond to this formula, oral corticotherapy (30-60 mg prednisone/day, depending on severity) will lead to remission.

Corticotherapy-resistant cases may respond to azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, cyclosporine or methotrexate.

●Fulminant colitis and toxic megalocolon

The careful monitoring of the patient is of paramount importance: fever, tachycardia, arterial hypotension, abdominal distension or sometimes only mild abdominal signs of peritoneal irritation may suggest the diagnosis of abscess or perforation in cases receiving corticotherapy in high doses. Ultrasound, CT, plain abdominal radioscopy/radiography and blood leukocyte count are performed several times a day for the early detection of free air in the peritoneal cavity (perforation).

In addition to endovenous perfusion, transfusion when needed, and corticotherapy, nasogastric suction or, more effectively, long intestinal tubes placed endoscopically are used in the case of important intestinal distension.

The following are contraindicated: narcotics, antidiarrheals, and anticholinergics. Medical treatment will not be extended for more than 48-72 hours, and in case of an unfavorable evolution, this will be replaced by surgical treatment.

Surgical treatment has the followingindications of principle:

-failure of medical treatment;

-disease complications;

-in pre-pubertal children (colectomy will improve stature-weight

retardation).

Unlike Crohn’s disease, in ulcerative colitis, surgery plays a curative role!

Surgical indications can be grouped into two categories: indications for elective surgery and indications for emergency surgery.

- Indications for elective surgery:

1. Lack of response to medical treatment

2. Malignization

3. Increased risk of malignization (dysplasia)

4. Extra-intestinal manifestations

5. Stature-weight retardation in children.

- Indications for emergency surgery:

1. Fulminant colitis resistant to medical treatment

2. Toxic megacolon

3. Perforations, abscesses

4. Important hemorrhage

5. Acute bowel obstruction.

Surgical procedures:

  • The following procedures are used for elective surgery:

1.Total proctocolectomy with ileostomy that involves the resection of the entire colon and rectum. The residual ileal stump is externalized to the anterior abdominal wall (ileostomy). The purely technical difference from the similar procedure for cancer is that the dissection plane, the release of the intestine is performed at the limit between this and the mesentery (in oncologic surgery, the mesentery is raised ]oop [o\;”in block” with the colic piece). Also, at the abdominal time, the rectum is mobilized in a plane close to it, in order to maintain the erector nerves intact; the perineal dissection of the rectum is performed in intersphincterial plane by another surgical team working concomitantly with the first. 2.Total colectomy with ileo-recto-anastomosis: It has less frequent indications, in cases with mild or no rectal involvement. Disadvantages: the possibility of the appearance of ulcerative proctitis in the residual rectum, the risk of its malignization and the great number of soft stools (it is contraindicated in patients with poor sphincter tone).

Fig.24:a. total colectomy with ileo-rectal anastomosis; b. total proctocolectomy with terminal ileostomy 3.Total colectomy with the stripping of the rectal mucosa and ileo-rectal anastomosis: a more recent procedure, consisting of the detachment and excision of the rectal mucosa over a 5-6 cm length above the dentate line (the perineal team); after colectomy and low rectal resection up to 5-6 cm from the anal orifice, the abdominal team will prepare an ileal reservoir to be anastomosed to the anal canal, after the telescoping of the ileal stump through the rectal stump with the stripped mucosa.

Ileostomy can be prepared in several different ways: simple, terminal, with a continent reservoir (Koch), with a J or S-or W-shaped reservoir.

Fig.25: a. accomplishing the W-shaped ileal reservoir (1,2,3, the three joined bowel loops; b. reservoir accomplished (black arrow), emergent ileal segment to be anastomosed with the rectum – or exteriorized as terminal ileostomy (white arrow).

  • Under emergency conditions (toxic megacolon, fulminant colitis,

hemorrhage, perforations), the most frequently used procedure is subtotal colectomy with ileostomy.

COLONIC DIVERTICULOSIS

Doru Munteanu

It consists of multiple herniations of the colonic mucosa, through the fibers of the colon muscle tunic up to the peritoneal serosa.

EPIDEMIOLOGY

The highest (and increasing) incidence is found in developed countries (USA, Australia, United Kingdom) and is proportional to age. It is dominant in men.

MORPHOPATHOLOGY

The colonic mucosa penetrates the circular muscle layer of the colon at the level of minimum resistance areas, generated by colonic parietal fenestrations through which the nutrient blood vessels penetrate towards the submucous plexus. Diverticuli are anchored between the mesenteric and the antimesenteric tenia, at the level of the sigmoid and descending colon.

Fig.26: Gross apearance – multiple large sigmoid diverticuli

PATHOGENY

The majority of the cases are generated by chronic intracolonic overpressure, which occurs in chronic constipation (low-fiber diet).

Other cases are due (like in abdominal wall hernias) to a collagen defect or other disturbances of the colonic parietal structure which, fragilized, will allow the herniation of the mucosa through the muscle fibers even at normal intracolonic pressures.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS

It should be emphasized from the beginning that colonic diverticulosis has no specific manifestations; moreover, it is completely asymptomatic for a long time period. Then follows a period when the only manifestations are: abdominal discomfort, borborygmus, a change in the rhythm and nature of defecation. Pain is cramping, of variable intensity, localized in the left iliac fossa and may last for hours or days, being exacerbated by food and partially relieved after defecation or gas emission.

Diverticulitis occurs when the feces that fill the diverticula become dehydrated, hard and they remain fixed at intradiverticular level, eroding and inflaming the diverticular wall. The process starts at the entrance of the diverticulum and subsequently extends to the entire diverticulum, sometimes to adjacent tissues.

EVOLUTION. COMPLICATIONS

Diverticulitis and peridiverticulitis may become complicated by peridiverticular abscesses (blocked perforations); repeated inflammatory episodes can generate colonic stenosis and intestinal partial or even complete obstructions; free perforation into the peritoneal cavity (peritonitis) is rare, but severe. Perforations usually occur gradually, without any pause to allow the adjacent viscera to attach to the colonic segment with diverticula, which results in fistulas with the vagina, urinary bladder, small intestine or skin surface.

The most frequent are the colo-vesical fistulas in men (in women they are less common, the uterus being interposed between the rectum and the bladder, and fistulas occur after hysterectomy).

Once formed, the abscess causes fever, localized pain, suprajacent muscle defense or thickening, sometimes a palpable painful tumor mass, hyperleukocytosis.

Lower digestive hemorrhage occurs when a fecalith erodes the mucosa, particularly a blood vessel at the level of the diverticular neck. Most frequently (80%), the hemorrhagic episode spontaneously stops; however, hemorrhage can sometimes be abundant, requiring emergency surgery.

PARACLINICAL DIAGNOSIS

Irrigoscopy/irrigography is effective in the detection and the determination of the extension of diverticulosis. Barium will opacify the diverticula that will appear round, clear-cut on the screen or on the film; in this way, the possible fistulas resulting from an inflammatory complication can also be opacified and evidenced.

Computed tomography successfully evidences the thickened areas of the colonic wall, the strictures; if a contrast substance has been ingested which has opacified the intestine (or mild contrast enema has been performed in order to avoid distension and perforation), CT can also detect potential extraluminal collections (abscesses).

Abdominal ultrasound may also provide useful information (colonic wall, intra-abdominal collections, fistulas) at a much lower cost.

Colonoscopy provides accurate information regarding mucosal changes, possibly the source of hemorrhage, but does not provide data on pericolic changes. It is extremely important that endocolic pressure during the exploration does not increase excessively (risk of perforation). Colonoscopy is essential in the detection of other lesions (benign, malignant tumors) concomitant with diverticulosis.

Angiography is important through the catheterization of the lower mesenteric artery and the opacification of this and its branches, in the detection of the source of bleeding. This can also be detected by the injection of a small amount of erythrocytes from the patient (previously labeled with Tc99m), followed by multiple scans; the procedure is effective in the detection of small intermittent hemorrhages, which are missed by angiography.

TREATMENT

In clinically manifest but uncomplicated cases, a fiber-rich diet will improve symptomatology by the shortening of the intestinal transit time and the reduction of endocolic pressure. Glucagon (2 mg i.m.) has proved to be effective in relieving pain, particularly in the case of the association of intestinal spasms.

Diverticulitis has a drug therapy indication in principle. A water diet will be maintained. Broad-spectrum oral antibiotics (amoxicillin) will be administered for at least 10 days. Severe cases require hospitalization, nasogastric suction for the resolution of distension, antibiotics to cover the spectrum of aerobic gram-negative germs (E. coli) and anaerobic gram-negative germs (Bacteroides fragilis) – gentamycin and tobramycin associated with clindamycin or mezlocillin.

Surgical indications in diverticulitis

1. Two or more diverticulitis episodes

2. Immunodepressed patients

3. Long duration corticoid treatment

4. The first attack of diverticulitis occurring at less than 40 years of age

5. Subocclusive syndrome (incomplete obstruction)

6. Impossibility to exclude cancer

7. Fistulas.

Indications for emergency surgery

1. Generalized peritonitis (free perforation or abscess)

2. Abundant bleeding

3. Intestinal occlusion.

Surgical procedures used

The aim of surgery is to remove the colon segment with diverticula. Most frequently, these are located in the sigmoid or descending colon, so that a segmental sigma resection (which should be extended caudally to the rectum in order to “raise” the potential spastic area that generates diverticula upstream) or left hemicolectomy will be sufficient.

The modality of finalization after the excision time will vary depending on the quality of the residual stump. After elective excision, in a prepared, evacuated and disinfected colon, the restoration of the digestive tract continuity by colorectal anastomosis is the routine procedure.

The situation is different in the case of emergency surgery, in an unprepared colon and/or in peritonitis or pericolic abscess. This requires extreme caution and after excision, the closure of the distal stump and the externalization of the proximal stump in the form of temporary colostomy, with the restoration of digestive tract continuity after 6-8 weeks under better local and general conditions.

Diverticular hemorrhage stops spontaneously in 80% of cases. In the rest of 20%, this requires more drastic measures. After the selective catheterization of the lower mesenteric artery, continuous intra-arterial perfusion with vasopressin (0.2-0.4 units/min), which stops hemorrhage in 90% of the cases, is tempting and effective (particularly in very elderly and multiple deficiency patients). However, in these cases, hemorrhage tends to recur sooner or later. Nevertheless, an extremely useful clinical delay is obtained for the re-equilibration of the patient and the preparation of the colon, so that surgery can take place under optimal conditions, with minimal risks.

Colon Cancer

Florin Graur

The colon is that part of the digestive tract located between the ileo-cecal valve and the colorectal junction and is divided into the following segments: caecum, ascending colon, hepatic flexure (or right flexure), transverse colon, splenic flexure (or left flexure), descending and sigmoid colon respectively. The sigmoid colon continues with the rectum at the colorectal junction.Of practical, surgical importance, a division based on colon’svascular supply is also used; hence, the part of the colon irrigated by branches originating from the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) is denominated as “the right colon” (caecum, ascending colon, right flexure and the right half of the transverse colon), while the left half of the transverse, the left flexure and the descending colon, irrigated by branches originating from the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA), are generally known as “the left colon”. The right colon is vascularized by the ileo-biceco-appendicular, right colic and middle colic arteries. The veins follow the arteries and drain into the superior mesenteric vein (and further in the portal vein). The left colon is vascularized by the left colic artery and sigmoid arteries. The veins follow the arteries and eventually drain into the inferior mesenteric vein (a splenic vein or portal vein affluent). Lymphatics also follow the vascular branches.

Both the ascending and descending colon are close attached to the posterior abdominal wall by the Told’s fascia.

Epidemiology and etiology

Colonic cancer has a rising incidence, average 32-68 per 100.000 inhabitants, especially in developed countries mainly due animal fat rich-food and low in dietary fibers, with a maximum level of incidence at the age of 70-80 years. Animal fats promote an exacerbation of anaerobic flora and transformation of bile salts in carcinogenic agents. Fibers on the other hand, reduce the bile salts action on colonic mucosa.

A number of diseases are considered as promoters for colonic cancer:

1. adenomatous polyps: adenomatous polyps have a proven evolution

towards cancer colic. The risk of malignancy is directly proportional

to their number and size (≥2cm in diameter).

2. intestinal polyposis

a) Familial adenomatous polyposis :

  • malignancy occurs at the age of 30. It is an autosomal dominant disorder.
  • associated with hypertrophy of the retinal pigment layer (screening test!). b) Gardner syndrome – associates, besides familial polyposis, desmoid tumors located in the midgut or abdominal wall and bone tumors. 3. ulcerative colitis – the risk of cancer increases with the lenght of the disease evolution and extent of lesions. 4. Crohn’s disease

Carcinomas of the colon can be divided as hereditary and sporadic. The hereditary type occurs in patients with family adenomatous polyposis (FAP) or hereditary non-polyposic colorectal cancer (HNPCC), while the sporadic type is generated by environmental factors.

Diagnosis

Clinical diagnosis

Colon cancer clinically manifests depending on the tumor location, with different clinical characteristics on the right colon compared to the left colon. Right colon cancer mainly manifests by anemia, a palpable tumor mass, diarrhea and fever. Tumors located in the left colon manifests by abnormal transit until the appearance of intestinal obstruction. Rectosigmoidian syndrome could be identified: rectorrhagia; tenesmus; blood, pus or mucus in the stool.

Also malignant syndrome is associated, manifested by weight loss, fatigue, loss of appetite, low grade fever, pallor. Complications of colonic tumors may manifest clinically by jaundice and hepatomegaly (secondary to liver metastasis), ascites and carcinomatosis nodules (in the case of peritoneal carcinomatosis), peritonitis (in perforations), intestinal obstruction (because of obstructing tumors).

Imaging and lab tests

Colonoscopy + biopsy

Colonoscopy highlights colonic tumors, specify their location, their appearance (polyploid, infiltrative or ulcerated) and allow the harvesting of biopsy for histopathological examination. Moreover, colonoscopy could treat potential pre-neoplastic pathology like polyps by endoscopic resections. If a total colonoscopy cannot be achieved (to exclude other colonic lesions), a virtual colonoscopy is indicated using computed tomography. If this examination is not available barium enema is performed.

Barium enema

Barium enema also highlights the tumor location, it can specify if there are multiple lesions, stenotic character, but cannot take biopsies.

Blood samples

Laboratory tests are useful for evaluating liver function, kidney function, presence of other diseases (diabetes). The CBC (cell blood count) provides information about anemia and infection and tumor markers are useful for monitoring treatment effectiveness.

Chest X Ray

Chest radiography may show the presence of lung metastases, but also other concomitant diseases.

US

Abdominal ultrasound can raise the suspicion of colonic tumor,by highlighting colon wall thickening, but is not specific. Instead it may reveal peritumoralcollections or in the peritoneal cavity because of colon perforations. Also it is very useful in highlighting and characterization of liver metastasis and raising suspicion of peritoneal carcinomatosis.

CT

Computer tomography, especially with contrast, highlights the tumor location, its stenosing character, presence of complications (perforation, obstruction), presence of other intra-abdominal injuries (liver metastases, carcinomatosis) or remote lesions (lung metastases, metastases in other sites). Also in some cases it can replace total colonoscopy by a virtual colonoscopy (without being able to harvest biopsies).

MRI

It provides essentially the same details on the tumor and its complications, as well the liver metastases or other organs as computer tomography.

PET

It is especially useful in detecting metastasis and relapse after radical treatment. It is not used routinely in colon cancer diagnosis.

CEA

Carcinoembryonic antigen (as well as other tumor markers) is used to monitor postoperative colon cancer, being used in initial diagnosis. It is measured preoperatively and is postoperatively reevaluated at predetermined time range. If the value decreases, it follows that the treatment was radical. If the value increases at subsequent checks it means that there was a relapse or metastasis and should be identified and treated.

Differentials

For the right colon cancer: pseudotumoral form of appendicitis, appendicular tumors, Crohn’s disease, ileo-cecal tuberculosis, other intraabdominal tumors.

For the left colon cancer: diverticular disease, granulomatous colitis, other intra-abdominal tumors.

Complications

Colon cancer can cause liver metastasis in approximately 70% of patients with this condition. Of these 50% are located only in the liver, but can otherwise occur in the lung or other organs. Only 10-25% of liver metastases are resectable.

In tumors located in the left colon tumor may cause obstruction or supratumoral perforation or at the caecum (diastatic perforation) – with symptoms of fecal peritonitis.

Tumors located in the right colon produce most often anemia, because of bleeding, but also it could cause obstruction in tumors located at the ileocecal valve.

Pathways extension of colon cancer are: lymphatic – with metastasis in lymph nodes; intraluminal – seeding tumor cells in colic segments located downstream; invasion – by infiltrating neighboring organs; peritoneal dissemination – with the appearance of peritoneal carcinomatosis; blood streamdissemination – the way of the portal vein, with the appearance of liver metastases, lung and other organs.

Liver metastases could be resected, thus realizing a downstaging and increasing the survival of the patients in stage IV.

Treatment

Colic cancer treatment is divided into radical treatment (surgical) and palliative treatment (endoscopic, oncological and symptomatic).

Surgical treatment

Radical treatment

Preparation for surgery includes mechanical preparation that is done with macromolecular solutions (Fortrans, Macrogol) and antibiotic prophylaxis.

The objectives of radical surgical treatment of colon cancer are: removal of colon segment with the tumor, with 10 cm of proximal and distal normal colon (safety edge oncology) and afferent mesocolon to achieve a more extended lymphadenectomy.

Depending on the tumor location, the following types of surgeryare performed:

  • Right hemicolectomy (resection include last loop of ileum, caecum,

ascending colon, right colic flexure and first third of the transverse colon). Restoring digestive transit is done through an ileo-transverso-anastomosis. This procedure is indicated for tumors located in the caecum until proximal third of the transverse colon.

Fig.27: a. segmental ileo-cecal resection; b. right hemicolectomy; c. segmental transverse colon resection; d. left hemicolectomy; e. segmental sigmoid resection

  • Segmental colectomy on transverse colon withcolo-colic anastomosis

is indicated in tumors located in the second third of transverse colon

  • Left hemicolectomy (resection includes the distal third of transverse colon,

left colonic flexure, descending colon with or without sigmoid, completed with transverso-sigmoido-anastomosis or transverso-rectal anastomosis or terminal colostomy and closing the distal stump. This intervention is indicated in tumors located from the left colonic flexure to the descending colon or sigmoid.

  • Segmental sigmoidectomy is indicated in tumors located in the sigmoid

colon and restoration of digestive tract is performed through a colorectal anastomosis. In some cases terminal colostomy with closure of the rectal stump (Op. Hartmann) is performed.

Palliative treatment

Palliative surgery is done in situations where the primary tumor cannot be removed, when it produces an obstacle on digestive transitor perforations with peritonitis. These procedures are classified inexternaland internal derivations.

Palliative operations are those who do not remove the tumor, which is not resecable, only by-passing the tumoral obstacle. Also palliative surgery could be done when the tumor is locally resecable, but with distant metastases (liver, lung etc.) and presents with complications (obstruction, perforation, hemorrhage).

Fig.28: a. ileo-transversostomy; b. loop ileostomy

External derivations are done upstream of tumor colic, and depending on the seat of the tumor can be: cecostomy – at the caecum; transversostomy – at the transverse colon level; sigmoidostomy – on the sigmoid colon. Colostomy bag is placed over the colostomy to capture thefeces for the hygiene and patient comfort.

Internal derivations achieve a by-pass of the region where the tumor lies. This can be achieved by ileo-transverso-anastomoses (for cancers located between the caecum and the proximal third of the transverse colon) and transverso-sigmoido-anastomosis (for cancers located between distal third of the transverse colon and the descending colon).

For perforated cancers or for diastatic perforations colonic resections are indicated, but in most cases an anastomosis is avoided, the surgeon preferring to do a colostomy with the closure of the distal stump, due to peritonitis.

In the patients with hemorrhagic colon cancers, also resections are indicated, but also the anastomosis will be at risk because of anemia.

Postoperative complications

The most important complication after colonic surgery is anastomotic fistula which eventually leads to peritonitis. This complication was reduced by preoperative colon preparation and the use of mechanical staplers.

Endoscopic treatment

Endoscopic treatment is useful in situations where the patient presents with obstruction due to tumor and it is performed by inserting a transtumoralstent to release the obstruction. By this method the patient can be operated in a single surgical procedure, not in successive surgeries. In addition the patient could be operated as elective surgery, after preparation, not as emergency.

Oncologic treatment

Oncological treatment use chemotherapy that is given before surgery (neoadjuvant) or postoperative (adjuvant) depending on tumor staging. Some single-agent chemotherapy is used: 5-FU, Vincristine, Irinotecan, Oxaliplatin, Capecitabine, Bevacizumab, and Cetuximab, but most often multiagent chemotherapy is indicated: FOLFIRI: folic acid, 5-FU, Irinotecan; FOLFOX: Oxaliplatin, 5-FU, Leucovorin; 5-FU with Vincristine.

Pathomorphology

The macroscopy reveals vegetating tumors, ulcerative vegetating or infiltrating (scirrhous).

The characteristic microscopic appearance isliberkuhnianadenocarcinoma with varying degrees of differentiation.Rarely, the pathologist can find mucinousor anaplastic carcinomas.Sarcomas or lymphomas are exceptionally rare.

Follow-up

The patients should be followed-up for at least 2 years: at three monthsan abdominal ultrasound, Chest X-Rays and CEA; at 6 months – CT scan and colonoscopy. After the initial 2 years a yearly follow-up should be done until 5 years.
